comparator.name: Applied Mathematics
comparator.sourceNotes: The formally adopted 2026-2027 appendix defines a 165-ECTS Applied Mathematics major and 15-ECTS minor. Year 1 is a compulsory 60-ECTS common Mathematics/Applied Mathematics foundation. The remaining 120 ECTS comprise 105 ECTS of major requirements and 15 ECTS of genuine minor space. First-year Project Applied Mathematics is used because it directly represents the named degree. For the two required project choices, Project Mathematical Modelling and Project Systems Theory are selected as the first two options in official order. Numerical Linear Algebra and Advanced Systems Theory are likewise the first two options in the required advanced-choice group. Statistical Modelling is the first Applied Mathematics elective not already used. These choices are fixed independently of UCR fit, and the open minor remains unpopulated. The official programme page and adopted appendix were rechecked on 2026-10-14; the settled curriculum and neutral choices remain unchanged. alternatives.labelRationale: The completed curriculum is dominated by mathematics, programming, algorithms, data, optimisation, linear systems, machine learning and robotics, with a smaller sustainable-technology application strand. The label does not claim proof-based analysis, topology, functional analysis, partial differential equations or Applied Mathematics project formation.

alternatives.concept: Combine mathematical and computational models with Earth-system science, geospatial and laboratory investigation, water–mineral interactions, resource recovery, climate mitigation and renewable-system assessment. This implements the target-linked mathematics-in-engineering-and-physics direction through available natural-system applications without claiming an Applied Mathematics curriculum.

alternatives.labelRationale: Six Earth and environmental courses replace six specialist algorithmic courses, producing a natural-system, resource and sustainable-technology curriculum while keeping quantitative modelling central. The label does not imply Applied Mathematics, physics or engineering equivalence.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Six courses, or 45 EC, differ in each direction. Optimisation, computer networks, algorithms, advanced algorithms, AI decision-making and reinforcement learning are replaced by Earth-system modelling, Dynamic Earth, soils and aquifers, environmental biogeochemistry, resource recovery and advanced resource research. These changes implement a natural physical-systems direction rather than threshold-filling substitutions.

alternatives.concept: Study living and human systems through molecular biology, physiology, neurobiology, laboratory work and disease mechanisms, combined with calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods, signals, probability, programming, machine learning and image analysis. This implements the target-linked biological-modelling direction through related quantitative bioscience rather than a mathematical-biology or Applied Mathematics curriculum.

alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Against the autonomous-systems route, fourteen courses (105 EC) differ in each direction; against the Earth-and-energy route, thirteen courses (97.5 EC) differ in each direction. The third programme replaces most specialist algorithms, autonomy, Earth, resource and energy study with molecular, physiological, neurobiological, laboratory and disease science, as required by the medical-technology direction.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both develop programming and computational problem solving; UCR uses general Python programming rather than a mathematics-specific scientific-programming course.
Both develop formal logic and discrete mathematical structures; UCR applies them to decision-making and algorithm construction rather than reproducing Groningen's proof-based sets-and-numbers course.
Both establish calculus and equation-solving foundations; UCR also introduces matrices, eigenvalues, complex numbers and differential equations.
Both address optimisation; UCR focuses on search and constraint-satisfaction methods for AI rather than a full applied-mathematics optimisation course.
Both directly study systems of equations, vectors, matrices and linear spaces; Groningen continues to a second dedicated linear-algebra course.
Both study root-finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, differential-equation methods, accuracy, stability and efficiency.
Both analyse linear systems through differential equations and state-space or related representations; UCR does not continue to Groningen's advanced systems-theory sequence.
Both use mathematical and algorithmic methods for computational problems; UCR emphasises algebraic algorithms and optimisation rather than the full Groningen computational-science component.
Both establish probability concepts and distributions; UCR combines probability with statistical inference and simulation.
Both develop statistical models; UCR teaches regression, classification and machine-learning methods rather than Groningen's dedicated Statistical Modelling elective.
Both extend calculus beyond the introductory level; UCR includes multivariable calculus, complex-valued functions and differential equations but not the target's full analysis sequence.
